headline: Another NZ Sawmill to Close as Claymark Exits Te Kūiti
pageTitle: Another NZ Sawmill to Close as Claymark Exits Te Kūiti | Saw Point November 2026
description: Saw Point November 2026: Claymark's Te Kūiti sawmill closure, China log demand, India's trade agreement, building consents, Karioi biocoal and forestry diesel costs.
summary: November's Saw Point covers the Claymark Te Kūiti sawmill closure, stronger China log demand, improved India trade access, building consents, new processing proposals and rising diesel costs.
coverAlt: Saw Point Issue 004 November 2026 original cover by Forest Products Exchange

sections.heading: THE BIG STORY: ANOTHER NZ SAWMILL TO CLOSE AS CLAYMARK EXITS TE KŪITI
paras: Claymark has announced the closure of its Te Kūiti sawmill, with 35 positions reportedly affected.
The mill has been processing approximately eight to ten truckloads of logs each day, with that volume expected to be redirected to Claymark's Rotorua and Katikati operations.
The closure comes as forests planted across the Waitomo district around 30 years ago are reaching harvest age.
While some production may be absorbed by Claymark's remaining operations, Te Kūiti will lose an established processing facility, along with the employment and local business activity it supports.
Logs previously processed locally may also need to travel further, adding transport costs and changing supply arrangements for forest owners.

Another regional mill closure is a concerning development for New Zealand's wood-processing industry, particularly when there is already pressure to retain processing capability and add more value to our forestry resource.

sources.text: Stuff / Waikato Times, 30 October 2026

sections.heading: MARKET UPDATE: CHINA LOG DEMAND PICKS UP AFTER GOLDEN WEEK
paras: China's log market strengthened through October.

Daily softwood log consumption was running above 60,000 m³ following Golden Week. Port inventory increased by approximately 120,000 m³ to 2.5 million m³, largely reflecting reduced consumption during the holiday while shipments continued arriving.
Laurie Forestry reported a CFR log price of around US$132/m³ in mid-October.
Chinese domestic selling prices also improved, with Laurie reporting average log trader losses narrowing from around US$6–7/m³ to approximately US$4/m³.
Consumption has improved, although trading margins remain tight.

sources.text: Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, October 2026

sections.heading: EXPORT WATCH: INDIA TRADE ACCESS IMPROVES, BUT PRICE STILL MATTERS
paras: The New Zealand–India Free Trade Agreement came into force on 20 October 2026, removing tariffs on more than 95% of current forestry and wood exports to India.
The agreement improves market access for New Zealand timber exporters, including processed wood products.

For sawn timber, there's no shortage of enquiry from India. From what we're seeing commercially, price expectations are often below levels that make supply from New Zealand viable, particularly once freight is included.
Improved market access is welcome, but converting that interest into commercially sustainable orders remains the challenge.

sources.text: NZ Government, 20 October 2026
WPMA
Laurie Forestry

sections.heading: DOMESTIC WATCH: BUILDING CONSENTS IMPROVE ANNUALLY, BUT MONTHLY ACTIVITY EASES
paras: Stats NZ reported 41,091 new dwellings consented in the year ended September 2026, up 18% on the previous year.
However, September's seasonally adjusted monthly figure fell 7.9%, following a 5.3% increase in August.
Non-residential building consents totalled $8.7 billion over the year, down 3.1%.
The annual residential figures are encouraging, although the monthly decline shows the recovery is uneven.

Building consents are a useful forward indicator for timber demand, but construction is only one part of the wider timber market. Consents also take time to translate into actual building activity and timber orders.

sources.text: Stats NZ: Building Consents Issued, September 2026

sections.heading: INDUSTRY WATCH: NEW LIFE PROPOSED FOR KARIOI PULP MILL
paras: The former Karioi pulp mill site near Ohakune could return to industrial use under a proposal to manufacture biocoal from forestry material.
Te Ara Hiko is proposing a facility capable of producing up to 180,000 tonnes of biocoal annually, using an estimated 500,000 tonnes of pulp logs and wood residues.
The project would reuse existing industrial infrastructure, with consents still under consideration.
If developed, it could create a substantial domestic market for lower-grade logs and forestry residues in the central North Island.

sources.text: Wood Central: Biocoal Plant Proposed for Former Karioi Pulp Mill, October 2026

sections.heading: INDUSTRY WATCH: MODULAR TIMBER MANUFACTURING FACES A TOUGH MARKET
paras: The final liquidation report on Evergreen Modular, released in October, highlights the difficulty of establishing offsite timber construction businesses in New Zealand.
The company entered administration in 2024 after investing in factory-built timber housing.
Offsite manufacturing offers opportunities to improve construction productivity, but factories need a consistent flow of projects to cover equipment, facilities and operating costs.
Investment in technology is important. So is having enough reliable demand and workable margins to keep production running.

sources.text: Wood Central: Evergreen Modular Liquidation, October 2026

sections.heading: ONE TO WATCH: DIESEL COSTS ARE EATING INTO FORESTRY RETURNS
paras: Higher diesel costs continue to put pressure on harvesting and log transport.
Laurie Forestry's October report estimated diesel at approximately $3.16/L for the month to date, compared with $1.81/L in October 2025.

The report estimates harvesting crews and log transport operators consume more than 300 million litres of diesel annually. At those prices, the additional annual fuel cost could exceed $400 million if sustained.

FICA's October market update also reported continued pressure on forestry contractors' profitability from rising fuel and freight costs, despite improving export log prices and strong harvesting activity.
Log prices may be firmer, but higher operating costs are absorbing a significant share of the return.

sources.text: Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, October 2026
FICA: Market Update, October 2026

sections.heading: SAW POINT
paras: Another sawmill closure is concerning, particularly when New Zealand is trying to develop more value-added processing.
The impact goes beyond the mill itself. Local transport operators, contractors, engineering businesses and other suppliers all depend on these operations.

The Evergreen Modular liquidation also shows that investing in new manufacturing technology doesn't guarantee a commercially viable business. Processing needs reliable demand, competitive operating costs and enough volume to justify the investment.
The proposed Karioi biocoal plant offers a different possibility, creating a new market for lower-grade logs and residues while reusing existing industrial infrastructure.
New Zealand needs more commercially viable processing, whether that's sawn timber, engineered wood products or alternative uses for our forestry resource.
Once the infrastructure, skills and supporting businesses disappear from a region, rebuilding them isn't easy.

headline: Domestic Demand Hits Its Best Level in Years
pageTitle: Domestic Demand Hits Its Best Level in Years | Saw Point September 2026
description: Saw Point September 2026: NZ timber demand and building consents, log export returns, China and India trade, and WorkSafe wood dust standards.
summary: New Zealand sawmills report improved domestic demand, while export returns, China and India trade, and wood-dust standards remain in focus.
introduction: Welcome to Issue 002 of Saw Point, a monthly newsletter for people who work in, buy from, or care about the New Zealand timber industry.
openingQuote: Each month, Saw Point covers the market, the industry news worth paying attention to, and what it could mean for New Zealand timber.

sections.heading: THE BIG STORY: DOMESTIC DEMAND HITS ITS BEST LEVEL IN YEARS
paras: Sawmills across New Zealand are reporting their strongest winter demand in several years, according to the Wood Processors and Manufacturers Association.

Forward orders are increasing, and most domestic processors are planning an average 5% increase in sawn timber prices for September while removing the fuel surcharge that's been in place through winter.
The pipeline behind it is real: 40,581 dwellings were consented in the 12 months to June, and WPMA is now pushing for more timber use in government procurement on the strength of it.
It's a genuinely better set of numbers than domestic sawmilling has seen for some time.
The question worth sitting with is whether it's enough, and whether it comes fast enough, for mills that have been running on thin margins for years.

sources.text: Wood Central: NZ Sawmills See Demand Tick Up as Consents Top 40,000

sections.heading: MARKET UPDATE: EXPORT RETURNS HOLD STEADY AS FREIGHT AND FOREX WORK AGAINST EXPORTERS
paras: The PF Olsen Log Price Index held at $122 in August, still $2 above the two-year average and $3 above the five-year average.
At Wharf Gate, export log prices were unchanged from July.

Ocean freight remains elevated and the NZD strengthened against the USD through August, both of which put downward pressure on returns. Offsetting that, modest gains in Chinese log prices have kept the index steady.

Combined with the domestic demand picture above, August looks like a market finding its feet on two fronts at once: export pricing holding its ground, and the local order book improving for the first time in a while.

sources.text: PF Olsen: Log Market - August 2026 via interest.co.nz

sections.heading: EXPORT WATCH: CHINA STEADY DESPITE A SLOWING ECONOMY, INDIA'S TRADE DEAL STARTS TO BITE
paras: Laurie Forestry's August report describes the last six months of export markets in one word: stability.
That continued in August, with China improving $1 to $3 per m³ at the wharf gate and India holding steady just ahead of China on price.
CFR pricing for A-grade logs into China moved up into the USD 125 to 130 per JASm³ range.

What stands out is that this is happening against a weakening Chinese economy. The manufacturing PMI fell to 48.5 in July from 50.4 in June, and GDP growth slowed to 4.3% year-on-year, the softest in three years.
Wood use is improving even as the broader economy cools.
India tells a more complicated story.
The log market itself remains subdued through the monsoon period, with weak sawn timber demand, unsold inventory and port congestion squeezing sawmill margins there.
But the wider trade picture is shifting.

New Zealand's wood product exports to India reached $193 million in the year to June, according to figures carried in WPMA's August newsletter, and Indian buyer enquiries at NZ sawmills have risen in the weeks since the India Free Trade Agreement was signed in Delhi.
The catch is where that value sits.
Logs alone still account for $122 million of the total trade with India, meaning a large share of it is unprocessed.

WPMA wants the processed lines carrying more of the trade as the deal comes into full effect, and the next couple of quarters of enquiry data will show whether that shift is actually happening or whether India simply becomes a bigger outlet for raw logs.

sources.text: Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, August 2026
Wood Central: NZ Wood Exports to India Triple Before Trade Deal Takes Full Effect

sections.heading: ONE TO WATCH: SOFTWOOD MILLS KEEP THEIR DUST LIMIT AFTER WORKSAFE ENDS REVIEW
paras: New Zealand's softwood processors will keep working to a wood dust exposure standard of 2 milligrams per cubic metre after WorkSafe dropped its plan to merge the softwood and hardwood dust standards into a single, tighter value.
WPMA confirmed the outcome, noting the hardwood standard has doubled to 1 milligram per cubic metre instead of softwood being pulled down to match it.
Processors had been watching the review closely, since a merged standard would have meant new dust control investment and compliance costs across softwood mills nationwide.
It's a straightforward win for processors on a cost line that rarely makes headlines but adds up in capital and operating spend when it moves.
Worth knowing if you run or supply into a mill: no new equipment or process changes forced by this one, at least for now.

sources.text: Wood Central: Softwood Mills Keep Their Dust Limit After NZ WorkSafe Ends Review

sections.heading: SAW POINT
paras: August is a genuinely more encouraging month than most of this year has offered.
Demand is up, forward orders are up, and mills are confident enough to plan price increases into spring.
That's worth acknowledging on its own terms, after a year that has also seen the sector lose capacity at Kaitāia and elsewhere.
But better demand doesn't undo what's already gone.
It changes the outlook for the mills still standing. It doesn't bring back the ones that closed.
The industry that meets this recovery is a smaller one than it was in January.

sources.text: Wood Central: NZ Sawmills See Demand Tick Up as Consents Top 40,000

headline: Red Stag Moves Modular Timber Onto the Factory Floor
pageTitle: Red Stag Moves Modular Timber Onto the Factory Floor | Saw Point August 2026
description: Saw Point August 2026: Red Stag's modular timber construction, NZ export log prices, India trade, Kaingaroa processing and sawmill pressures.
summary: Red Stag’s modular timber development, export log prices, India trade and New Zealand wood processing investment.
introduction: Welcome to Saw Point. A monthly newsletter for people who work in, buy from, or care about the New Zealand timber industry.
openingQuote: I’m George Harman. I am the director of Sutcliffe Trading, a timber broking business operating since 1988, and I’m the founder of FPX. Each month, Saw Point will cover the market, the industry news worth paying attention to, and what it could mean for New Zealand timber. July gave us plenty to start with.

sections.heading: THE BIG STORY: RED STAG MOVES MODULAR TIMBER ONTO THE FACTORY FLOOR
paras: July marked a significant step for Red Stag’s move into modular timber construction.

The first four VoMo mass timber modules were assembled at Red Stag’s Rotorua operation, forming a demonstration building. One of the modules is being fitted out as a premium hotel room for inspection by an international hotel operator.
The system uses cross-laminated timber as the structural shell, with rooms manufactured and fitted out in the factory before being transported to site.
The important part for the timber industry is where the value is being added.
Instead of stopping at a log, sawn timber or even an engineered timber panel, the fibre moves further through the value chain into a finished building component.
New Zealand has talked about adding more value to its radiata resource for a long time. This is a practical test of whether that can be done competitively at scale.

sources.text: Wood Central: Red Stag Builds Its First Fully Fitted Timber Modules Onshore

sections.heading: MARKET UPDATE: JULY RECOVERS SOME OF JUNE'S FALL
paras: Export log pricing improved through July after the drop seen in June.
Laurie Forestry reported more stable conditions across China and India, with lower shipping costs and favourable foreign exchange helping New Zealand wharf gate returns recover close to May levels.

PF Olsen’s late-July indicative North Island pricing showed Export A at NZ$118 per JAS m³ at wharf, Export KI at NZ$100 and Export KIS at NZ$91. Indicative domestic pricing showed P40 pruned logs at NZ$175 to NZ$202 per tonne at mill and S30 structural logs at NZ$120 to NZ$145.

There were some better domestic signals as well. July market reporting pointed to 39,737 new homes consented in the year to May 2026, up 19 percent, bringing an end to three consecutive years of decline in annual consent numbers.
There is some relief in those numbers, but it is too early to call it a strong recovery. July looks more like the market finding some footing after a difficult first half.

sources.text: PF Olsen: Current Log Prices and Carbon Market Data
Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, July 2026
Wood Central: NZ Log Prices Climb Out of Their Mildest Winter Dip in Four Years

sections.heading: EXPORT WATCH: INDIA IS GROWING, BUT IT IS NOT A SIMPLE SECOND MARKET
paras: India continues to attract attention as New Zealand looks to broaden its export options beyond China.

Laurie Forestry reported that Kandla is receiving around nine to ten softwood log vessels each month, with three to four typically coming from New Zealand. Each vessel carries around 40,000 cubic metres of logs on average.
That is meaningful volume, but the report also highlights the risks.

Congestion at Kandla can lead to significant unloading delays, with some vessel charterers paying more than US$1 million in demurrage. Laurie Forestry also warned about exporters sending logs into India without firm sales contracts and letters of credit in place.
India represents an opportunity, but it is not a market where volume should simply be pushed in and the sale worked out afterwards.
Relationships, contracts and control of supply matter.

China remains critical to New Zealand forestry. India gives the sector another option. The challenge will be developing that market without pushing too much volume into it before demand and relationships are ready.

sources.text: Laurie Forestry: Monthly Report, July 2026

sections.heading: ONE TO WATCH: KAINGAROA LOOKS AT PROCESSING MORE AT HOME
paras: A proposed integrated wood processing hub at Kaingaroa moved into a six-month feasibility phase during July.

Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Manawa and NZ Bio Forestry are exploring a model that could combine sawmilling, advanced wood processing, renewable energy and green chemistry near one of New Zealand’s major forestry resources.

The proposal includes finding higher-value uses for material across the processing chain, including mill residues that could eventually feed products such as biochemicals and sustainable aviation fuel.
It is still early. Commercial viability, investment, regulatory approvals, governance and community support all need to stack up before anything gets built.
But the model is worth watching.
Process more close to the forest. Use more of the fibre. Create more value before the product leaves the region.

sources.text: Wood Central: Ngāti Manawa Rallies Kaingaroa and Murupara Behind NZ’s Bio Hub Bid

sections.heading: SAW POINT
paras: July put two very different processing stories side by side. In Rotorua, Red Stag is investing in taking radiata pine further through the value chain. In Kaitāia, Juken confirmed the closure of its Northland Mill after a buyer could not be found, putting 60 jobs at stake.

The issue is not whether New Zealand has enough wood. It is whether processing businesses can remain competitive through energy costs, construction cycles, export conditions and the capital required to modernise.

Watch the investment going into new processing, but also watch the capacity disappearing at the other end. Both will shape how much value New Zealand can continue to add to its timber before it leaves the country.

sources.text: Wood Central: Red Stag Builds Its First Fully Fitted Timber Modules Onshore
Wood Central: Juken Loss Nears $40 Million Behind Its Northland Mill Closure
